strengths: Large-scale pretraining on 229,619 public CT series with a two-stage SSL (DINOv3-style) + VLA (SigLIP) pipeline adapted to volumetric CT, demonstrating a practical path to open CT foundation models.

Architectural innovations for volumetric CT: anisotropic 3D tokenization, 3D RoPE with jittering, and a local-global transformer design that makes full-volume attention computationally tractable while preserving local detail and global context.

Strong empirical results on several downstream tasks: best performance on 4/6 cancer biomarker benchmarks under frozen kNN evaluation, competitive encoder-only segmentation with SEoMT, and substantial zero-shot retrieval gains on CT-RATE (e.g., R@100 59.9 vs. 28.8 for CT-CLIP).
Comprehensive supplementary material detailing datasets, preprocessing, hyperparameters, hardware, and additional experiments, supporting reproducibility.
Open-source release of code and model weights, which is valuable for the medical imaging community.
weaknesses: Data leakage is a serious concern: pretraining on NLST likely includes the LUNA16 evaluation set (LUNA16 is derived from NLST), and pretraining on AMOS likely includes the AMOS22-CT segmentation evaluation set. The paper does not exclude these overlaps, so results on LUNA16 and AMOS22-CT are likely inflated and not comparable to prior work.

Overclaiming: The abstract/conclusion state that SPECTRE 'consistently outperforms prior CT foundation models,' but Table 3 shows Merlin outperforms on Findings R@8 (98.8 vs. 93.5) and Impressions R@8 (85.4 vs. 72.8), and Table 1 shows SPECTRE underperforms nnU-Net ResEnc L on KiTS23 (86.64 vs. 88.06), LiTS (80.14 vs. 81.20), and WORD (83.31 vs. 85.79). Claims need qualification.

Missing ablations on the paper's core architectural contributions: there is no controlled study isolating the benefits of local-global attention, 3D RoPE, anisotropic patch size, or the two-stage pretraining design. The only ablation is limited to optimizer, crop size, and SSL vs. VLA initialization on one segmentation dataset.

Reproducibility inconsistency: the window partition is unclear. The text states a full scan is partitioned into G=36 windows of size 128×128×64 voxels, but a 512×512×384 scan would require 96 such windows. This inconsistency affects the claimed computational tractability and makes the method harder to reproduce exactly.
The 'Scaling' claim in the title is not substantiated by experiments: only a single model size (339M local + 58M global) is trained, with no scaling laws or comparisons across data/model sizes.

Evaluation breadth is limited in places: fine-tuned segmentation comparisons do not include other CT foundation models, small datasets (NSCLC-Radiogenomics, Colorectal-Liver-Metastases) have wide confidence intervals and no significance tests, and the zero-shot retrieval results on Merlin are mixed.

Text augmentation via LLM rewriting (Gemini 2 Flash) is used to generate report paraphrases without clinical verification, which may introduce factual noise and irreproducibility, and its effect is not ablated.

strengths: Comprehensive, multi-task evaluation spanning six biomarker classification benchmarks (frozen kNN), four volumetric segmentation datasets, and two zero-shot text-to-image retrieval benchmarks, which provides reasonable evidence that the learned representations transfer across heterogeneous downstream objectives.

Zero-shot text-to-image retrieval results are notably strong: on CT-RATE, SPECTRE achieves Recall@5 = 17.5 versus 2.9 for CT-CLIP, and it substantially improves over CT-RATE on Impressions-to-Image retrieval, indicating meaningful cross-modal alignment.

The model is trained exclusively on publicly available CT data (229,619 series across NLST, CT-RATE, INSPECT, MerlIn, AMOS, PANORAMA, AbdomenCT-1K), and the authors state they will release code and pretrained weights, which materially aids reproducibility and reuse.

Architecture design is thoughtfully motivated by CT-specific constraints: anisotropic 3D patch embeddings (16x16x8) aligned to voxel spacing, 3D RoPE with DINOv3-style jittering for variable spacing/FOV, and a local/global transformer split that keeps attention tractable for whole-scan context.

The two-stage SSL-then-VLA pretraining pipeline (DINOv3/iBOT/KoLeo followed by SigLIP alignment with a Qwen3-0.6B text encoder and LoRA adapters) is a sensible and reasonably novel combination for volumetric medical data, and the use of sigmoid-based SigLIP to handle noisy many-to-many image-text pairs is well-justified.
Related work is thorough and clearly positions SPECTRE against prior CT foundation models (CT-CLIP, MerlIn, CT-FM, FMCB, VISTA3D, PASTA, VoCo, MedImageInsight, etc.).
Limitations are discussed candidly, including thoracic skew of the pretraining corpus and the smoothing behavior of the encoder-only segmentation head.
weaknesses: Technical novelty is limited: the method is essentially a careful recombination of existing components (DINOv3 self-distillation, iBOT masked distillation, KoLeo regularization, SigLIP loss, 3D RoPE, hierarchical local/global ViT), with domain-specific adaptations rather than new algorithmic ideas. The paper itself describes the goal as keeping the architecture 'as close to the plain ViT architecture as possible,' which reinforces this concern.

The headline claim that SPECTRE 'consistently outperforms prior CT foundation models in both zero-shot and fine-tuned settings' is not fully supported. On segmentation (Table 1), SPECTRE (87.55 AMOS-CT, 86.64 KiTS23) does not outperform nnU-Net (88.87, 88.06) or nnU-Net ResEnc L (88.06, 81.20), and the text honestly frames this as 'competitive,' which conflicts with the abstract's framing.

Biomarker classification gains (Fig. 1, Fig. 3) come with wide 95% confidence intervals, and SPECTRE does not reach SOTA on NSCLC-Radiomics and Colorectal-Liver-Metastases. The 'best on 4/6' claim therefore rests on differences whose statistical reliability is unclear from the main paper.

Key architectural and objective choices are not ablated in the main text. There is no ablation isolating SSL-only vs VLA-only vs the combined two-stage recipe on the biomarker benchmarks, and no ablation of the anisotropic patch size or RoPE jittering, even though these are presented as central design contributions.

No computational cost analysis (FLOPs, latency, memory) is provided despite the paper repeatedly emphasizing efficiency and tractability of large-scale 3D attention; this weakens the 'efficient 3D transformer' framing.

The retrieval comparison on MerlIn (Table 3) is mixed: SPECTRE substantially underperforms MerlIn on the Findings-to-Image task (55.5 vs 77.6 at K=1, N=32). While the paper explains this via domain overlap, it does temper the cross-modal alignment claims.

The pretraining corpus is heavily skewed toward thoracic imaging, which the authors acknowledge could confound the comparison; the lung-dominated benchmarks (LUNA16, DLCS, NSCLC) may be advantaged in ways that make cross-benchmark rankings harder to interpret.

Fairness of the segmentation comparison is only partially controlled: baseline numbers are drawn from other papers (Wald et al., Ji et al.) with differing training protocols and split conventions, so the encoder-only SPECTRE comparison is not fully apples-to-apples.

strengths: The pretraining corpus is substantial (229,619 CT image series assembled from publicly available datasets), and the authors commit to releasing the model, training code, and recipes, which is a genuine community resource for volumetric medical imaging.

The evaluation is broad: six biomarker-classification benchmarks against eleven CT foundation models, four segmentation datasets, and zero-shot CT–report retrieval on two datasets, with a clearly described frozen-embedding kNN protocol and per-task confidence intervals.

The supplementary material is unusually thorough (data filtering, coordinate/geometry normalization, LLM report rephrasing, LoRA configuration, hardware, and hyperparameters), which aids reproducibility.

The engineering choices for scaling 3D attention (local window ViT with per-window [cls] tokens, pooled window descriptors feeding a small global ViT, 3D RoPE with jittering, and anisotropic 16×16×8 patching) are sensible and non-trivial adaptations of ViT components to CT geometry.
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty. SPECTRE is essentially a composition of existing ingredients—DINOv3 self-distillation, iBOT, KoLeo, SigLIP, 3D RoPE, and a local/global attention split—applied to CT. The paper itself states the goal is to keep the architecture 'as close to the plain ViT architecture as possible.' No new objective, representation, or insight is introduced that would not be predictable from the cited works.

Overclaimed results. The abstract states SPECTRE 'consistently outperforms prior CT foundation models,' yet it loses on two of six biomarker tasks (NSCLC-Radiogenomics, Colorectal-Liver-Metastases) and underperforms Merlin on Findings-to-Image retrieval (e.g., 55.5 vs 77.6 Recall@1 at N=32 in Table 3). The 'consistently' framing is not supported by the reported numbers.

Segmentation is not competitive with the state of the art. Table 1 shows nnU-Net and nnU-Net ResEnc L clearly ahead on every dataset, with an especially large gap on KiTS23 (86.64 vs 99.79). Describing these numbers as 'competitive' in the text overstates the evidence.

The retrieval gains over CT-CLIP are implausibly large (e.g., 59.9 vs 28.8 Recall@100 in Table 2), which raises questions about whether the comparison is apples-to-apples (CT-CLIP uses a different image encoder and possibly different preprocessing/splits). No analysis is provided to rule out protocol or model-mismatch effects, and this is precisely the result on which the 'cross-modal alignment' claim rests.

Ablation and analysis are thin. Table 7 only studies optimizer and crop size on a single dataset (KiTS23). There is no ablation isolating the contribution of the local/global design, 3D RoPE, the two-stage SSL→VLA pipeline, or the individual SSL objectives, so the claimed importance of each design choice is not empirically established.
There is little mechanistic understanding of why the representations transfer better. The saliency maps (Fig. 4) and UMAP (Fig. 7) are purely qualitative and are not tied to any quantitative claim.

The resource requirements (24 Blackwell B200 GPUs, 4.32 TB GPU memory) are extreme, and the paper does not discuss the compute/carbon tradeoff or whether the performance gains justify the scale, which is relevant for a 'scalable' foundation-model claim.

Several claims are asserted rather than demonstrated—e.g., that geometric priors 'need to be introduced by design,' that the two-stage pipeline 'combines the strengths' of SSL and VLA, and that the model 'preserves spatial discriminability'—without controlled experiments that would isolate these effects from raw data scale.

strengths: Large-scale open-data pretraining: 229,619 CT series from public datasets; two-stage DINOv3/iBOT/KoLeo SSL followed by SigLIP VLA with Qwen3 text embeddings; a local-global ViT design with anisotropic 3D tokenization and 3D RoPE that directly targets CT-specific challenges such as anisotropy, token scaling, and weak supervision.

Broad empirical evaluation: six biomarker benchmarks with frozen kNN, multiple segmentation benchmarks (KiTS23, LiTS, WORD, TotalSegmentator), and zero-shot CT-RATE/MERLIN retrieval. Results show strong gains in several settings, e.g., CT-RATE text-to-image Recall@5 17.5 vs CT-CLIP 2.9, and best or competitive performance on 4/6 biomarker tasks.

Detailed architecture and training recipe: the paper clearly describes local/global attention aggregation, RoPE frequency allocation, DINO/iBOT/KoLeo losses, SigLIP alignment, data preprocessing, hyperparameters, and hardware, which aids reproducibility.

Useful ablations and analyses: Table 8 studies optimizer, crop size, and SSL vs VLA initialization; Table 10 compares linear, SEoMT, and UNETR decoders and small-lesion behavior; retrieval robustness to token/span dropout and report length is analyzed.

Open and clinically motivated: explicitly avoids private data, uses public CT corpora, and positions the model as a general-purpose CT foundation model, which is valuable for the medical imaging community.
weaknesses: Potential benchmark contamination: NLST is included in SSL pretraining, while LUNA16 (and likely other NLST-derived chest benchmarks) is a subset of NLST. The manuscript does not report excluding overlapping scans/patients from pretraining, so the LUNA16 and potentially DLCS biomarker results may be inflated. This is a material evaluation flaw that should be corrected with scan-level exclusion or at least explicitly analyzed.

Limited methodological novelty: SPECTRE is primarily an engineering combination of existing components (DINOv3, iBOT, KoLeo, SigLIP, 3D RoPE, local-global ViT). There is no controlled compute-matched comparison or ablation isolating the proposed local/global design, 3D RoPE, anisotropic tokenization, or SigLIP versus InfoNCE, making it difficult to attribute gains to the architecture rather than scale/data.

Overclaiming relative to evidence: the abstract/conclusion claim 'consistently outperforms prior CT foundation models in both zero-shot and fine-tuned settings,' but Table 9 shows SPECTRE below CT-FM (87.34 vs 89.81 on TSv1-Full) and below Merlin (87.29 vs 90.17 on TSv2-Merlin), and Table 3 shows MERLIN Findings retrieval far below Merlin (e.g., Recall@1 55.5 vs 77.6 at N=32). The claims should be qualified.

Evaluation limitations: biomarker prediction uses frozen kNN rather than fine-tuning or true zero-shot classification, and segmentation uses an encoder-only EoMT decoder that is not optimized for dense prediction. The comparisons therefore do not fully establish the model's fine-tuned or dense-prediction superiority. CT-RATE retrieval compares mainly to CT-CLIP, not all foundation models.

Reproducibility/access concerns: the main-paper code link is blank/placeholder, and the LLM-based report rewriting with Gemini 2 Flash plus Qwen3 LoRA text encoding may be difficult to reproduce exactly. Training requires 24 B200 GPUs, so practical uptake is limited unless pretrained weights are actually released and documented.

Statistical strength: some reported advantages in Figure 3 have overlapping 95% confidence intervals (e.g., C4KC-KiTS, Colorectal-Liver-Metastases), so 'outperforms on 4/6' should be interpreted cautiously and supported with significance tests or more detailed per-task statistics.

strengths: Introduces SPECTRE, a fully transformer-based 3D CT foundation model trained on a very large, fully open corpus (229,619 CT series across NLST, CT-RATE, INSPECT, Merlin, AbdomenAtlas, AMOS, PANORAMA, AbdomenCT-1K), which is a meaningful scale for medical imaging and avoids reliance on private data, lowering barriers for the community.

Combines DINOv3-style SSL with SigLIP-based vision-language alignment using paired radiology reports in a coherent two-stage pipeline, and the design choices (asymmetric patch sizes, 3D RoPE with DINOv3-style jittering, local/global two-stage attention with window-level aggregation) are motivated by concrete properties of volumetric CT (anisotropy, cubic token growth, quadratic attention cost).

Evaluation is broad and reasonably fair: 11 CT foundation models compared across six biomarker benchmarks using a standardized frozen-embedding kNN protocol, four segmentation benchmarks (plus TotalSegmentator-based TSv1/TSv2 subsets), and zero-shot retrieval on CT-RATE and Merlin. The paper also provides ablations on optimizer, crop size, decoder variants (Linear/SEoMT/UNETR), and robustness to text dropout.

Reproducibility is strong: code is released, pretraining recipes are provided, hyperparameters and dataset filtering criteria are detailed in the supplement, and downstream fine-tuning is largely delegated to standard nnU-Net pipelines.

Qualitative evidence (saliency maps in Fig. 4, UMAP in Fig. 7, segmentation visualizations in Fig. 6) supports the claim that the learned representations encode clinically meaningful spatial structure without task-specific fine-tuning.
weaknesses: The headline claim of superior biomarker classification performance is weaker than presented: the radar plot (Fig. 1) and bar chart (Fig. 3) show substantial overlap of 95% confidence intervals across models, and SPECTRE is not best on 2/6 tasks (NSCLC-Radiogenomics, Colorectal-Liver-Metastases). The paper reports means but no significance tests, so 'consistently outperforms' is not fully supported by the reported evidence.

The retrieval story is mixed rather than uniformly strong. In Table 3, on Merlin's own benchmark, SPECTRE is substantially worse than Merlin on the Findings section (55.5 vs 77.6 at N=32) and comparable-to-worse at high recall on Impressions (93.5 vs 98.8 at K=8). The paper acknowledges this, but the abstract/discussion framing ('substantially outperforms', 'robust visual-textual grounding') overstates the cross-modal alignment gains, which are driven mainly by the combined Findings+Impressions setting and by the use of LLM-rewritten text augmentation.

Segmentation performance is competitive but not clearly SOTA: on TSv2-Full, SuPreM (86.95) and CT-FM (89.81) outperform SPECTRE (88.85 is actually higher than SuPreM... wait, CT-FM at 89.81 is best), and on TSv2-Merlin CT-FM (90.17) again leads. The claim that SPECTRE 'surpasses all domain-specific transformer-based models' is true for KiTS23/LiTS/WORD but the encoder-only formulation trails strong convolution-based baselines, which the authors correctly note but which tempers the 'scalable general-purpose' framing.

Technical novelty is largely integrative: the method combines existing components (DINOv3, iBOT, KoLeo, SigLIP with LoRA on Qwen3 embeddings, 3D RoPE) with modest architectural changes (mean-pooled window aggregation, learnable class queries). The paper does not isolate which design choice drives the gains via controlled ablations of the geometry-aware components versus the SSL/VLA objectives in the main text.

Several design and evaluation choices could bias comparisons: text is rewritten/expanded with Gemini 2 Flash (three paraphrase variants) and the model uses Qwen3-0.6B embeddings with LoRA rather than a fixed text encoder, which may advantage SPECTRE on retrieval relative to baselines using original reports. The very low MedSigLIP retrieval (0.3-8.2%) suggests the protocol may be sensitive to text-side configuration, yet no analysis of this sensitivity is provided.

Reported gains on the primary biomarker benchmark are modest in absolute terms (e.g., LUNA16 0.92 vs ~0.88 for FMCiB/ModelsGenesis, DLCS 0.86 vs ~0.78) and it is unclear how much of this stems from the much larger pretraining corpus versus the proposed two-stage objective, since no compute/data-matched baseline is provided.

strengths: Addresses a genuinely useful problem with a well-motivated recipe: a two-stage SSL (DINOv3/iBOT/KoLeo) followed by SigLIP-style vision-language alignment for volumetric CT, with geometry-aware design choices (anisotropic 3D patching, 3D RoPE with jittering, windowed local ViT + global aggregation ViT) that are explicitly justified by CT-specific issues (token scaling, anisotropy, noisy reports).

Substantial and well-documented data engineering: a ~229,619-series pretraining corpus assembled from public sources (NLST, CT-RATE, INSPECT, MerlIn, AbdomenAtlas, AMOS, PANORAMA, AbdomenCT-1K) with per-dataset exclusion criteria, resampling/windowing protocols, and hyperparameters (Tables 4-6) that make the pipeline largely reproducible.

Broad, mostly harmonized evaluation: 11 CT foundation models compared on six biomarker benchmarks with frozen-embedding kNN under the TumorImagingBench protocol (Fig. 1, Fig. 3), plus segmentation on KiTS23/LiTS/WORD/TotalSegmentator subsets and zero-shot retrieval on CT-RATE and MerlIn. This is more comprehensive than most prior CT foundation-model papers.

Useful ablation and robustness analyses: decoder variants (Linear/SEoMT/UNETR) on KiTS23, crop-size and optimizer ablations (Table 8), native voxel-spacing robustness, and text token/span dropout (Fig. 8). The CT-RATE retrieval improvement over CT-CLIP (Recall@5 17.5 vs 2.9) and the encoder-only segmentation results are strong practical signals.

Honest limitation discussion: the authors acknowledge smoothing of small/faint lesions at 1/4 resolution, thoracic skew of the corpus, report noise/inconsistency across institutions, and the high cost of pretraining. Open-source release of weights/code is promised and lowers the barrier for reuse.
weaknesses: The headline claim is overstated relative to the paper's own tables. The abstract states SPECTRE 'consistently outperforms prior CT foundation models in both zero-shot and fine-tuned settings', but Table 3 shows MerlIn (a prior CT foundation model) clearly better on Findings retrieval (Recall@1 77.6 vs 55.5; Recall@8 98.8 vs 93.5), and Tables 1/9 show SPECTRE below nnU-Net ResEnc L on KiTS23/LiTS/WORD (86.64 vs 88.06; 80.14 vs 81.20; 83.31 vs 85.79), below SuPreM on TSv1-Full/TSv2-Full and below CT-FM on TSv2-Merlin. SPECTRE also loses 2/6 biomarker tasks. The claim should be scoped to 'competitive with/among the best' rather than 'consistently outperforms'.

The central methodological claim - that the two-stage SSL-then-VLA pipeline produces better representations - is not ablated on the primary benchmarks. There is no SSL-only vs VLA-only vs SSL+VLA comparison on the frozen-kNN biomarker tasks or on retrieval. Worse, the one relevant ablation (Table 8) shows that at the final 320x320x128 crop the VLA-initialized and SSL-only models are identical (0.871 vs 0.871), and the supplement notes the gap 'narrows, rendering them comparable'. Without this ablation, the main design contribution is unsubstantiated.

Several reported gains are marginal and likely within noise. The 95% CIs in Fig. 3 overlap heavily for many model/task pairs, no significance testing is reported, and two of the biomarker datasets are very small (NSCLC-Radiogenomics, 133 cases; Colorectal-Liver-Metastases, 194 cases), which the paper itself attributes to quantization noise. The evidence does not support strong ranking claims on the biomarker suite.

Methodological novelty is limited. Windowed local attention plus a global aggregation transformer with cls-token pooling, 3D RoPE with DINOv3-style rescaling/jittering, and a DINO+iBOT+KoLeo loss with SigLIP alignment are all existing components; the paper's own text frames them as 'an adapted version of the DINOv3 framework' and 'SigLIP-style'. The distinctive element is scale on CT, which is a legitimate but incremental contribution, and the 'exclusively openly available CT datasets' framing is not a differentiator (MerlIn, CT-CLIP, FMCB also use public data).

Possible pretraining/evaluation contamination is not addressed. AbdomenCT-1K is used for pretraining, yet it is explicitly described as aggregating public single-organ datasets (its constituent sources include LiTS and KiTS-style collections). The authors carefully drop AMOS to avoid contamination but apply no equivalent check for AbdomenCT-1K against the LiTS and KiTS23 evaluation sets, which could inflate the reported segmentation numbers.

The retrieval comparisons against non-CT-specific baselines are implausibly lopsided and unexamined. A 6x Recall@5 gap over CT-CLIP (17.5 vs 2.9), a model trained with a CLIP-style objective on ~25k chest CTs, warrants an analysis of protocol fairness (windowing, input extent, token budget, pooling) rather than a bare number. The MedSigLIP token-limit issue is discussed, but no such scrutiny is applied to CT-CLIP/OpenCLIP/BioMedCLIP, so the strength of the cross-modal result is uncertain.

The qualitative evidence for 'clinically meaningful' features is weak. Figure 4 presents occlusion-sensitivity maps computed at 1/4 feature resolution; they are coarse, blocky, and visually selective, yet the paper draws a strong conclusion ('the model already attends to pathologic regions associated with tumor presence') without quantification, without a comparison to a baseline, and while labeling the maps 'non-curated' in a way that cannot be verified from the PDF.

Reproducibility is partially constrained: the code footnote on page 1 is empty in the submitted version, pretraining required 24 B200 GPUs, and some design choices are asserted rather than justified (e.g., the per-axis frequency allocation d_k = 0 mod 6 in Eq. 10).
